body:
After weighing the three contributions, I see merit in combining elements rather than adopting any single proposal wholesale. The original account correctly spotlights the lack of a shared, durable reference (a written schedule) as a source of confusion, but the objection reminds me that the problem may also involve deeper relational dynamics that a mere spreadsheet cannot fix. The rival’s chore‑wheel idea offers a concrete, visual protocol that reduces reliance on memory and verbal agreements, and its log‑sheet component directly addresses the objection’s concern about a traceable record of exceptions. 

Thus, I propose a hybrid approach: (1) start with a brief, low‑stakes diagnostic talk to surface any underlying tensions or power imbalances; (2) agree on a visual chore‑wheel (paper or digital) that rotates weekly, complemented by a simple log of any swaps or deviations; (3) establish clear, enforceable ground‑rules for conflict resolution, including a short pause‑and‑share step and a defined consequence for repeated non‑compliance (e.g., temporary reassignment of the offending chore); (4) set a recurring 5‑minute check‑in (in‑person or via the shared board) to update availability and adjust the wheel; and (5) embed a feedback loop – a brief weekly satisfaction rating – to evaluate whether the system improves fairness and communication.  This blended model respects the need for an explicit coordination tool, acknowledges possible relational issues, and provides measurable ways to iterate.

I will leave the precise format of the wheel (paper vs. app) open pending the flatmates' technical comfort, and I will keep the evaluation criteria flexible so they can be refined after a trial month.
commitments: 1. Facilitate a short, neutral diagnostic conversation with all three flatmates to identify any relational or power‑dynamic factors beyond chore logistics. 2. Co‑design a visual chore‑wheel (printed poster or shared digital board) that assigns weekly responsibilities and includes a simple log for swaps, ensuring every roommate is comfortable with the chosen medium. 3. Draft a concise ground‑rules sheet that outlines the pause‑and‑share dispute process, specifies a concrete consequence for repeated breaches, and defines how chores will be rotated to maintain equity. 4. Schedule a 5‑minute weekly check‑in (or asynchronous update via the board) to capture schedule changes and adjust the wheel accordingly. 5. Implement a weekly satisfaction check (e.g., 1‑5 rating) and a brief review after the first month to assess the system’s effectiveness and decide on any adjustments.
